title: Trump visits the White House roof
description_short: Trump visits the White House roof
description_medium: During an August 5, 2025 visit to the White House roof, Trump surveyed the grounds with architect James McCrery, who was overseeing a proposed $200 million ballroom. Trump described the project as a way to spend his money and said private donors would cover it. The reports do not provide formal budget, approval, or historic-preservation records.
description_long: On August 5, 2025, Donald Trump made an unexpected walk on the White House roof, spending about 20 minutes looking over the roof and grounds, including the recently renovated Rose Garden. Architect James McCrery, who was working on a proposed 90,000-square-foot ballroom, joined him. The Associated Press reported that Trump pointed out parts of the property and told reporters he was considering “another way to spend my money for this country.” The White House had announced the ballroom project, estimated at $200 million, and Trump said he and private donors would pay rather than use government funds. The visit was a site review, not evidence that all project arrangements were settled. The linked reporting does not include a formal budget, donor commitments, an approval record, or historic-preservation review. Those documents would be needed to establish the final cost, funding terms, and authorization status.

preserved_fields.title: Trump visits the White House roof
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump visits the White House roof

notes: AP reports the roof visit, the announced $200 million ballroom, architect James McCrery’s presence, and Trump’s statement that private donors would pay. It does not provide formal budget or donor records, approval status, or historic-preservation review; those remain unresolved.

title: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland
description_short: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland
description_medium: On September 27, 2025, Trump federalized 200 Oregon National Guard members over the governor’s objection and sent them to Portland. A federal judge later found no lawful basis for the deployment under the cited statute, noting that protests at the ICE facility had been mostly peaceful for months. The court permanently barred the deployment.
description_long: On September 27, 2025, the Trump administration federalized 200 Oregon National Guard members over Governor Tina Kotek’s objection and deployed them to Portland, saying the mission was to address protests outside the city’s ICE facility. Oregon and Portland challenged the move. After a three-day trial, a federal judge concluded on November 7 that the administration lacked a lawful basis under 10 U.S.C. §12406 to federalize the troops. The court found that violent protests in June had quickly subsided and that later demonstrations were predominantly peaceful, with isolated low-level incidents. It also noted that local and state law-enforcement officials responsible for the facility had not requested the deployment. The court entered a final order against the federalization, and Oregon’s litigation tracker records the resulting injunction and later troop demobilization. The record describes a contested National Guard deployment and a court ruling on its statutory authority; it does not describe an invasion of Portland.

preserved_fields.title: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland

notes: The linked timeline is supplemented by the Oregon court’s November 7 order and the state DOJ litigation tracker. Those records state that 200 Guard members were federalized over the governor’s objection, the court found no lawful basis for the move, and the deployment was enjoined.

title: Billions in Defense Contracts to Trump-Affiliated Firms
description_short: Lawmakers requested DoD IG investigate billions awarded to Trump-affiliated companies. Critics cited extreme conflicts of interest and self-enrichment.
description_medium: The Washington Post reported that 15 companies backed by investment firms affiliated with Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump received $3.2 billion in federal contracts, investments, and loans, mostly after their father returned to office. Four Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon inspector general to investigate the awards. The figure also included $3.1 billion in future contract options.
description_long: The Washington Post reported on August 5, 2026, that 15 companies receiving investments from firms affiliated with Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump had obtained $3.2 billion in federal contracts, investments, and loans, most after Donald Trump began his second term. The sons were linked to 1789 Capital and American Ventures, which invested in defense-sector companies. The lawmakers’ letter cited an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options. Representative Robert Garcia and Senators Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Tammy Duckworth asked the Department of Defense inspector general to examine which awards involved Trump-family-linked companies, how award decisions were made, and whether officials followed ethics requirements. Their request followed reporting; it was not an inspector general finding that the awards were improper. The linked article and lawmakers’ letter do not report a completed investigation or a response from the Pentagon watchdog. The figures combine several types of federal awards and should not be read as $3.2 billion in completed defense contracts alone.

preserved_fields.title: Billions in Defense Contracts to Trump-Affiliated Firms
preserved_fields.description_short: Lawmakers requested DoD IG investigate billions awarded to Trump-affiliated companies. Critics cited extreme conflicts of interest and self-enrichment.

notes: The Post reports the $3.2 billion aggregate across contracts, investments, and loans and identifies 15 companies; the lawmakers’ letter also cites $3.1 billion in future options and requests an IG inquiry. No completed IG findings or response are reported.

title: The UN Security Council endorses the Gaza Peace Plan that had been
description_short: The UN Security Council endorses the Gaza Peace Plan that had been put forwarded by President Trump
description_medium: The Security Council adopted Resolution 2803 on November 17, 2025, endorsing Trump’s Gaza plan by 13 votes, with China and Russia abstaining. The resolution welcomed a transitional Board of Peace, authorized a temporary International Stabilization Force, and allowed a Palestinian committee to manage day-to-day administration. Its reference to Palestinian statehood was conditional.
description_long: On November 17, 2025, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the U.S.-backed Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. The vote was 13 in favor, none opposed, with China and Russia abstaining. The resolution welcomed a Board of Peace as a transitional governing body for Gaza and authorized it and participating states to establish a temporary International Stabilization Force. It also provided for a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to manage day-to-day governance and for reconstruction arrangements under the Board’s oversight. The text referred to a possible path to Palestinian statehood only if conditions were met, including reform of the Palestinian Authority and progress in Gaza’s recovery. The Guardian reported that the draft had been revised to include this conditional language. The resolution endorsed and authorized parts of the plan; it did not itself establish that the force had deployed or that the proposed governance arrangements were operating.

title: The US Court of Appeals for the DC circuit rules to put
description_short: The US Court of Appeals for the DC circuit rules to put
description_medium: A 2–1 panel of the D.C. Circuit declined to pause a lower-court order blocking the Trump administration’s expanded expedited-removal policy. Judge Jia Cobb had ruled that DHS could not apply the fast-track process nationwide to migrants unable to show two years of continuous U.S. presence. The appeals court kept most of that order in effect pending appeal.
description_long: On November 22, 2025, a 2–1 panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit declined to stay most of Judge Jia Cobb’s August 29 order in Make the Road New York v. Noem. That order blocked DHS from applying expanded expedited removal to noncitizens encountered anywhere in the United States who could not show at least two years of continuous presence. Under the expansion, migrants could face rapid removal without the usual immigration-court process. The appeals court denied the administration’s request to restore the broader policy while the case proceeded, citing concerns about due process and erroneous summary removal. It granted a narrower stay concerning changes to credible-fear procedures for people who remained eligible for expedited removal. The decision left the central nationwide expansion blocked during the appeal, while allowing that limited procedural change. The order addressed the administration’s request for a stay; it was not a final resolution of the underlying appeal.

title: Trump Org Revenue Soars 17-Fold to $864M in First Half of 2025 Due to Crypto
description_short: Trump Org Revenue Soars 17-Fold to $864M in First Half of 2025 Due to Crypto
description_medium: Reuters analysis published October 2025 found that Trump Organization income surged 17-fold from $51 million in H1 2024 to $864 million in H1 2025, driven almost entirely by cryptocurrency ventures including memecoin royalties and WLF token sales. Eric Trump and Don Jr. held secret pitch meetings with wealthy foreign investors offering $WLFI governance tokens for $20 million+ commitments. The NYT reported that WLF representatives used Signal to solicit secret multimillion-dollar payments from crypto startups in exchange for the privilege of 'associating with the Trumps.'
description_long: The linked CNBC article concerns a different revenue figure from the one in this record. It reports that Trump’s foreign real-estate licensing income reached $59.5 million in 2025, up 71 percent from 2024, based on a financial disclosure analysis. CNBC attributes much of the income to Gulf property projects, including payments associated with Saudi developer Dar Al Arkan and Dubai-based Damac. The article does not report $864 million in first-half Trump Organization revenue or analyze memecoin royalties and World Liberty Financial token sales. The existing populated summary cites Reuters and New York Times reporting about those separate claims, but those articles and their underlying revenue, token-sale, and solicitation records are not among the linked sources here. The CNBC page therefore cannot verify the title’s 17-fold growth or its asserted crypto drivers. The appropriate amount, accounting period, companies, and source documents for the crypto-related claim remain unresolved.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Org Revenue Soars 17-Fold to $864M in First Half of 2025 Due to Crypto

The NYT reported that WLF representatives used Signal to solicit secret multimillion-dollar payments from crypto startups in exchange for the privilege of 'associating with the Trumps.'

The existing summary cites different Reuters and New York Times coverage; those articles, revenue records, token-sale data, and investor-solicitation evidence are needed to support the title and summary.

title: Transition Team Fires Federal Workers
description_medium: Before Trump even officially took office, his transition team sent out notices terminating thousands of federal workers, attempting to enforce the 'Schedule F' classification early. The unprecedented and legally dubious move bypassed standard civil service protections and created chaos across federal agencies, jumpstarting his campaign to gut the 'deep state.'
description_long: The Guardian reported in February 2025 that thousands of federal probationary employees had received termination notices as part of the administration’s effort to reduce the workforce. It noted that the government had more than 220,000 probationary employees and described efforts to reverse some firings, including at the National Nuclear Security Administration and the Agriculture Department’s bird-flu response. The article also quoted workers who said the notices accused them of poor performance despite positive reviews. This report concerns notices sent after Trump took office and does not establish that his transition team fired employees before inauguration or that the action implemented Schedule F. The supplied source does not identify every affected employee group or confirm the number of completed terminations. It also discusses potential financial costs and legal challenges rather than presenting a final accounting of the government’s liability. The existing summary’s timing and attribution need correction, and personnel notices or agency records are needed to establish final termination counts.

preserved_fields.title: Transition Team Fires Federal Workers
preserved_fields.description_medium: Before Trump even officially took office, his transition team sent out notices terminating thousands of federal workers, attempting to enforce the 'Schedule F' classification early. The unprecedented and legally dubious move bypassed standard civil service protections and created chaos across federal agencies, jumpstarting his campaign to gut the 'deep state.'

notes: The linked Guardian report describes post-inauguration termination notices to probationary employees and reversals at some agencies. It does not support the existing summary’s claim that the transition team issued notices before Trump took office or that the notices enforced Schedule F. Agency notices and final personnel records are needed to confirm categories and completed terminations.

title: Hegseth Fires Another Batch of Generals
description_short: Hegseth Fires Another Batch of Generals
description_medium: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed another group of senior military officers in June 2025, continuing his purge of general officers he deemed insufficiently loyal to Trump's agenda. The latest dismissals included combatant commanders with decades of experience. Former defense officials warned that the hollowing out of experienced military leadership created readiness gaps at a time of multiple simultaneous crises including the Iran strikes and ongoing operations in Yemen.
description_long: CNN’s February 20, 2025 article said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth might fire more than six senior officers. Sources told CNN that the potential list included Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. CQ Brown and that the candidates were viewed as too political or too close to former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin. The article reported possible dismissals, not a completed June purge. A separate June 18 report described Hegseth’s dismissal of Gen. Timothy Haugh, who led the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command. At a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing, Hegseth said he was the decision-maker and gave no specific reason for Haugh’s removal; Senator Jackie Rosen questioned the decision and its consequences. These sources do not establish the June dismissal of multiple combatant commanders or provide a sourced readiness assessment showing gaps caused by the removals. The Senate exchange discussed the decision process, not operational readiness effects.
